item.title: A Preteen Trapped in the Crossfire Between Separated Parents
item.description:
Parenting

A Preteen Trapped in the Crossfire Between Separated Parents

How we can learn to put our kids first.

Posted May 4, 2026

I was mindlessly scrolling through social media the other day when a still image from a video on Instagram caught my attention.

It was a mom arguing with her preteen daughter in the car.

I was intrigued.

Above the post there was a heading:

This is the conversation every child from divorce deserves to hear (my italics)

Below the post:

Most parents never get here (with a crying emoji)

I read some background on the side bar. The scene was an excerpt from season 8 of the drama series “Desperate Housewives” aired in October 2011.

I pressed play.

The Background

The girl is glaring out the window of the front seat of her mom’s car as her mother is talking to her. The girl doesn't want to hear what her mom is saying.

The background is that her parents are separated, and the preteenager and her mom are arguing about the girl’s reluctance to get out of the car to meet with her father.

This isn’t a unique story. What is surprising is the position that the mom takes and the argument that she is making.

There is so much in this small exchange.

The Conflict

Girl: I thought we were going to the mall

Mom: No, sweetie, listen

Girl: Can we get out of here quickly

Mom: No, you need to spend some time with your dad

Girl: I don't want to

Mom: I’m not giving you a choice

Look at him

Look

You know why he’s sitting over there

Because he misses you so much

Girl: Then he shouldn't have left us for Jane

article continues after advertisement

Mom: That's not what happened

He didn't leave us

He left me

And he didn’t do it for Jane

He did it because...

We just don’t make each other happy

And then he met Jane

And I guess she does

Girl: But you said that...

Mom: I know I said a lot of things I shouldn't have

I’m sorry

There are no bad guys here

There are just people trying to figure things out

And there’s one of those people

The Exchange

This exchange is piercing and topical.

I’m not commenting on the ethical issues around whether it is right or wrong for the mom to pressure her daughter to do something that she is evidently uncomfortable with, and I’m not weighing in on the rights or wrongs of infidelity and the related notion of blame and punishment.

I’m describing a dialogue between a mother and daughter in the strong likelihood that this communication, or some version of it, is being played out at this very moment hundreds of times across the world.

There is little doubt that parental separation usually brings emotional turmoil for the child, including intense feelings of pain, guilt, abandonment, anger, loss, and confusion and it is not uncommon for children to be caught in the crossfire between their parents.

The Mother’s Reframing

My interest is in how this particular mother handles this particular situation and how she reworks her initial entrenched narrative to forge a new path for herself and her daughter. Clearly, the mother has decided to reframe her initial rigid version of the separation to one that favors flow, repair, and less judgment. She talks calmly and with feeling and respect toward her daughter.

article continues after advertisement

The mother expresses how she misread the situation on so many levels.

She explains to her daughter that her dad didn't leave both of us.

"He left me". This makes an important distinction between herself and her daughter. She is saying in simple language, you aren’t responsible for this, it’s between your father and me.

Then she clarifies and reorders her understanding of the previous timeframe.

"He left because we ( your dad and I ) just don’t make each other happy."

"And then he met Jane".

Then she replaces blame and judgment with truth, realism, and humanity: "There are no bad guys here. There are just people trying to figure things out."

The mother expresses regret about the previous remarks she made.

"I know I said a lot of things I shouldn't have. I’m sorry."

And she encourages her daughter to see her father and to consider that her Dad has feelings: "He misses you so much". The mother firmly introduces some softness and forgiveness into the space.

The mother is acknowledging that she has some responsibility for the situation and that she can no longer place all the blame on her ex. Rather, she is experiencing some remorse for some of the things she has said; she admits that she has made mistakes and that it's time to address and begin to repair some of her missteps.

There is something else at play here as the mother recognizes that her daughter is modelling her behaviour. She realizes that if this continues, the girl may end up trapped in a more generalized judgmental narrative, which is split into right versus wrong and does not allow for ordinary human failings and compassion. She doesn't want this for her daughter.

Instead, the mother is taking the opportunity to rewrite her own and her daughter’s life script. She moves from a position of blame, rigidity, and judgment toward one of repair, forgiveness, and safety, as the “bad guys” are transformed into humans who are just trying to “figure things out”.

The Mother Comes Into Her Agency

Paradoxically, by taking responsibility for her past behaviours, the mother grants herself agency. She becomes the "adult" in the room; she is no longer a victim who has been wronged, rather, she is a woman who can think and knowingly share some ownership for the breakdown of the marriage. She can be hurt and in pain, and she can also choose to move with these feelings rather than be paralyzed by them.

article continues after advertisement

This is neither an easy nor a quick process, but she is beginning to free herself in order to move forward.

She gives her daughter the gift of being able to witness an honest, raw, and potentially reparative experience in which she can have two parents who put her first rather than trap her in their own cycle of blame and anger.

More conversations like this are needed.

item.title: Working with Fears of Death
item.description:
Fear

Working with Fears of Death

Beyond avoidance of the fear of death.

Posted May 4, 2026

Key points
  • It's normal to think about death.
  • Working with our fears helps us move forward.
  • Working with thoughts, feelings, and coming into the moment are tools.

Death is part of being alive. And thinking about death is part of being human.

Unbidden thoughts arise—sometimes quietly, sometimes like a jolt—catching us off guard and unsettling our sense of safety.

Just the other day, I was soaking in a warm bubble bath when, out of nowhere, a thought flashed through my mind: At any moment, I could receive a dire diagnosis—and that would be it. The end of my life.

It stopped me cold.

These kinds of fears are not new to me. As a child, I would lie awake at night, terrified I might not wake up. I worried my heart would simply stop beating. Thankfully, my parents offered steady reassurance, and eventually that phase passed, as most phases do.

But the thoughts never disappeared entirely.

Now, as an adult, when fears of death arise, I wonder:

How would I cope?
Who would miss me?
Why is this coming up right now?
What should I do with this feeling?

Turning Toward, Not Away

Since learning about emotions and developing the Change Triangle, I’ve made a commitment: I tend to my emotions instead of automatically avoiding them.

I wasn’t always this way. Before I understood how emotions work, I struggled with clinical depression—twice. Now, working the Change Triangle is part of my daily self-care. It’s not just a tool for healing, it’s a tool for prevention.

Because here’s what I’ve learned: When we can be with our fears, they lose their power to haunt us. Death anxiety is a “toughie.” But it’s workable. Here are a few ways I meet it.

1. Use a Defense—On Purpose

Sometimes, the most skillful move is to gently set the thought aside. Avoidance gets a bad rap, but defenses are not the enemy—they are emotional protection. The key is using them consciously. If I’m in the middle of something important, I might say to myself: Not now. I’ll come back to this later. And often, the thought passes.

Nevertheless, the cost of avoidance is that deeper emotions and needs may go unattended. When we chronically avoid emotions, those feelings tend to resurface as symptoms like anxiety, physical tension, or depression.

So the question becomes: Is now a moment to set this aside—or a moment to turn toward it?

article continues after advertisement

2. Get Curious: What Is This Really About?

If the fear lingers, I shift from avoidance to curiosity.

I gently ask myself:

  • What exactly am I afraid of?
    Is it physical pain? Loss? Missing out on life? Leaving loved ones behind?
  • Why now?
    Did something happen—a loss, a conflict, a milestone—that stirred this up?
  • Is another emotion underneath?
    Sometimes fear masks something else. For example, I’ve noticed that anger can morph into a fantasy about my own death—followed by an imagined scene of someone feeling regret for hurting me. This happened more often in my teens.

3. Tend to the Emotions in the Body

From an AEDP perspective, emotions are not just thoughts—they are physical experiences. So instead of staying in my head, I drop my attention below the neck. With fear, I might notice:

  • A racing heart
  • Tightness in my chest
  • A fluttering or trembling sensation

Then I do something simple but powerful:

I stay with the sensation.

I breathe slowly and deeply with the technique of deep belly breathing. I let go of the storyline and focus only on the body. I track the feeling as it moves, intensifies, and softens.

Often, if I stay long enough, something shifts. The fear peaks—and then begins to release. Sometimes memories or images arise. Sometimes there’s clarity. Sometimes just relief. In AEDP, we call this riding the full wave of a core emotion until completion.

This is how we metabolize emotion. Working with emotions in this way is truly transformational.

4. Return to the Present Moment

Ultimately, the goal is not to eliminate thoughts of death—it’s to not get stuck in them. When fear has been acknowledged and processed, we can gently guide ourselves back to now.

Try this:

  • Feel your feet firmly on the ground
  • Take six slow, deep belly breaths
  • Look around and name:
    • 3 colors you see
    • 3 textures you notice
    • 3 sounds you hear

This grounds the nervous system and reminds us: Right now, I am alive and OK.

Thoughts about death are inevitable. But suffering from them is not. As Irvin Yalom (2008) reminds us, “Though the physicality of death destroys us, the idea of death may save us.” When we meet these thoughts with curiosity instead of avoidance, they guide us back to what matters most: connection to both our deepest self and to others, meaning, and being fully alive in this moment. We can build a deep and resilient capacity to face life’s hardest truths.

item.title: Control Versus Connection in Parenting and Teaching
item.description:
Parenting

Control Versus Connection in Parenting and Teaching

We blame children for being dysregulated in a disconnected world.

Posted May 4, 2026

Key points
  • When we control children according to "guidelines," we train them to lose a sense of their internal compass.
  • When teachers prize obedience and punish kids when it is not achieved, there is no space for individuality.
  • There is something beautiful about holding space for children to recognize who they are and what they want.

It is a scary and confusing time to be a parent. We hear that kids' mental health has been declining in the past few decades, with many pointing fingers at screens, video games, and social media. There are guidelines for "healthy" amounts of screentime, outdoor time, reading time, and more. I don't know about you, but I feel the pressure to adhere to these guidelines acutely. As in, if I'm not, then I am doing my child a disservice.

I think culturally we do our children a far greater disservice—in the form of control. Think of all the ways we associate control with good parenting (consider this concept in the frame of teaching as well). We believe our job is to force our kids to eat vegetables. And limit screentime. And participate in youth sports. And read books.

But control isn't safety. When you make a child eat another bite of broccoli that they don't want, it suggests that their internal readings of fullness and craving aren't important. When you tell a child they can't play the game they love, you indicate that their interests should be quashed. We think of it as training our children to lead a good life, when in reality, it is training them to lose a sense of their own internal compass. We teach them to override their signals. Perhaps we even teach those signals out of them.

This leaves our children without a strong sense of self. When children show low self-esteem, anhedonia, frustration intolerance, or emotional dysregulation, we then talk about those symptoms as characteristics of the child. It becomes part of their self-concept when, in reality, those symptoms are a reaction to their environment.

These are two sides of the same coin of control. Either we are regimenting our kids into what we perceive to be the right way to live, or we are pointing the finger at their symptoms and saying they need work. We dominate, then pathologize.

This goes for teaching as well. Some teachers prize obedience and use punishments when it is not achieved. The only way to be a good kid in this environment is to be a quiet kid who does what the teacher says. There is no space for individuality or self-expression in that.

Prioritizing the Relationship

What both of these approaches miss is connection. We, as parents and teachers, need to prioritize the relationship. We can see this in polyvagal theory. The ventral vagal pathway is our ideal state. It is activated when we feel safe, social, and connected. Interestingly, its nerves extend throughout the face, so the ventral vagal pathway guides our facial expressions and our ability to mirror others' facial expressions. You know when you talk to a friend, and they cross their arms, and you feel compelled to cross your arms? We mirror each other bodily as a way to connect with each other emotionally.

article continues after advertisement

When our kids do not feel that connection, either with us or with other authority figures in their lives, they go into a sympathetic response. This can manifest in the form of frustration or anger. Or, they have a dorsal vagal response, where they listen, obey, and numb their true feelings. We do too much of this; we ask so much of our kids without being grounded in connection first, keeping them in lower nervous system states. And when they are in these states, we make it even harder to connect with them.

What's the solution? Put away the guidelines. Loosen the structure. Lower the expectations. Let children have space to follow their internal signals—or what they want to eat, do, or not do. Then connect with them where they are. Be present.

There is something beautiful about holding space for children to recognize who they are and what they want in life. To be a safe, loving container for them to learn how to listen to their internal signals and take care of themselves. To me, this is the greatest form of parenting we can do.

Here is a story that exemplifies this point. Imagine a fourth-grade class with a teacher who does not prioritize connection. This teacher focuses on the surface-level aspect of the craft—getting the lessons taught, making the students line up, and getting home. Children know when they are safely connected or not. These students know that the teacher sees being with them as a job and that obedience is key. But some kids want to express themselves. For example, a child who loves to collect objects. He talks about how much joy objects bring him. This child finds a paperclip. The teacher tells him to throw it out. The student asks if he could put it in his locker, to which the teacher says you either throw it out or go to the principal's office. The perception is that the student is undisciplined and deserving of punishment.

Because the teacher does not choose connection, the student feels hurt and unseen. Then there are meetings about the child's behavior. About how scary paperclips are and how kids are not allowed paperclips (really?).

Adults often create a world that sounds scarier and more threatening as a way to make up for their inability to connect with a child and be with them where they are. They seek safety for kids through outside parameters (no paperclips, no walking by yourself) instead of recognizing their role in putting them in the heightened state. The child becomes a safety risk to control when it was the teacher who put the child in the sympathetic stress response in the first place.

article continues after advertisement

All of this can be avoided with connection. And what's sad to me is that the child is the one who loses. We blame children for being dysregulated in a disconnected world. The child questions themselves and their self-worth. They learn they cannot be trusted to do the safe or right thing. We hurt our children's self-concept because we fumble our interactions with them. It is pathologizing the child for their reaction to our control.

Parents and Teachers Lacking Connection

We can zoom out further and say that parents and teachers need more connection, too. It's hard to impossible to model connection when we are under financial duress, physically unsafe, and mentally exhausted. When we lack connection, it is harder for us to show up and provide connection to them. We all end up living in a lonely world.

In the past few years, the inner workings of power, corruption, politics, and big business have been brought to light courtesy of the Me Too movement, the Epstein files, and more. No longer are patriarchal, capitalistic ideals considered impregnable. It is time we recognize the way patriarchy and a winner-takes-all attitude have bled into our parenting and teaching practices, such that we prioritize achievement and obedience over who our children actually are. We need to start using mental health symptoms in a child to identify where we haven't made them feel safe. And it is time for us to take responsibility for those behaviors, modeling what accountability—not control—looks like.

The open question for me is how we talk with authority figures in our children's lives who do not understand the importance of connection, or who believe they are connected. We know our kids don't feel emotionally safe in this person's presence, yet we are powerless to change the dynamic, especially if it's in the context of school or other essential institutions. We can try to tell our children to let it go, learn how to exist with transactional people, and more. But it doesn't solve the problem. Perhaps these are hard situations that will help our children identify how they do not want to act in life. But that doesn't make it any easier to watch.

article continues after advertisement

We all need each other more than we need guidelines. We need safety and space to express our individuality without judgment. This will support our mental health more than any guideline ever could.

item.title: How Strong Feelings Can Mislead Us About Truth
item.description:
Neuroscience

How Strong Feelings Can Mislead Us About Truth

We should be cautious about strong feelings of certainty.

Posted May 4, 2026

Key points
  • Perceptions that seem obviously true are, at best, only partial reflections of reality.
  • We feel good when we perceive what we expect to perceive but upset when our expected perceptions are wrong.
  • Feelings are fallible guides to knowing that our perceptions are true.

Normally, it seems like we see the world the way it really is—that our perceptions of the world correspond accurately to reality. But how do we know that our perceptions are really true?

Research by Anil Seth suggests that the brain constantly predicts what we are going to see next, and as long as those predictions match incoming sensory information, our sense is that we are seeing the world the way it really is. All of the colors, shapes, sounds, and movements of objects that we sense are perceived to be "out there" as real features of the environment, not figments of our imagination.

However, neuroscience tells us a different story, that everything we perceive to be "out there" is actually a fictional construction of the brain, a way of interpreting the world that helps us to deal with the environment but not literally reflecting external reality.

The biologist Jakob von Uexküll used the term Umwelt to refer to an animal's perceptual world, and pointed out that the brains of different species are tuned in to only the aspects of the environment that are important for survival and reproduction. Bees, but not humans, can perceive ultraviolet light, allowing them to navigate, even on cloudy days. Bats, but not humans, can perceive ultrasonic frequencies to orient themselves in space. It is clear that every species, including humans, constructs an internal representation of the environment based on only a tiny fraction of reality. The map is not the territory.

Even though our perceptions are fictional constructions, they do need to correspond to reality to some degree. If we perceive a tree as open space, we will walk into it. If we are throwing a spear at an animal that is 20 feet away but seems to be 40 feet away, we will miss it. If a plant tastes deliciously nutritious but is poisonous, we will die. The brain must therefore have some way of signaling us when our perceptions are on or off target.

The Feeling of Knowing

Neuroscientists have identified the dorsal anterior insula in the right temporal lobe of the brain as the area that informs us about the failure of the brain to predict incoming information. Such failures generate a sense of surprise and consternation, which motivates us to try harder to figure out what is going on. In contrast, when there is no discrepancy between what our brains are predicting and incoming information, we experience what Robert Burton called "the feeling of knowing" in his book On Being Certain.

The feeling of knowing is a strong emotion that arises when people are convinced that they have the right answer to a question—even when they have the wrong answer, or no answer at all. Research has shown that when people believe that they've had a sudden insight into the solution to a problem (sometimes called an "aha!" or "Eureka! experience), there is a burst of electrical activity in the anterior superior temporal gyrus of the right temporal lobe of the brain. It does not matter whether the felt insight is correct or incorrect; the strong emotion makes people particularly confident that they are in possession of certain truth.

article continues after advertisement

Ecstatic Epilepsy

An even more dramatic sense of certainty occurs in cases of ecstatic epilepsy. Ecstatic epilepsy is a blissful state of mental clarity and feeling of certainty that occurs just prior to a seizure in the right temporal lobe of the brain. Unlike the aha! moment, ecstatic epilepsy is not the consequence of believing one has solved a specific problem. Rather, it is simply a profound feeling of having universal truth revealed, similar to a mystical or religious experience. Researchers hypothesize that the cause of the experience is a suppression of signals in the dorsal anterior insula in the right temporal lobe that normally inform a person about prediction errors. The suppression of thoughts about errors leads to a feeling of perfect certainty and truth, however ineffable. The same phenomenon can be created by electrical stimulation of the dorsal anterior insula in people who do not suffer from ecstatic epilepsy.

The moral of this story is that strong feelings and convictions about possessing truth should not be trusted blindly. One might even say that the stronger the feeling of certainty, the more caution we should use. Our brains are doing the best that they can to allow us to get by in the world, but the brain is far from infallible. Understanding this point can help us to avoid acting on mistaken perceptions of the world, especially misjudgments of other people,
